questions.text: Human factor engineering is defined as the study of humans and their interaction with

options.c: The tools that they use and the environment

questions.explanation: The tools that they use and the environment. Human factors engineering (HFE) is formally defined as the scientific discipline concerned with understanding the interactions between humans and the elements of a system — specifically the tools, equipment, tasks, and environments in which people work. The goal is to optimize human well-being and overall system performance by designing systems that fit human capabilities and limitations. Option A is too narrow and partially inaccurate. Option B (demographic and organization) has no basis in HFE science. Option D describes outcomes of poor HFE design, not the definition. Per the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society (HFES), AHRQ human factors guidance, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, the correct definition centers on humans and their interaction with tools and environment.

questions.text: A hospital decided to open Palliative care and involve the staff in learning. One of the major things is to adopt best practice, train staff, and take to visit the other facilities. What would be the best to support this action:
questions.explanation: High level of strategic planning. Opening a palliative care service, adopting best practices, training staff, and benchmarking through facility visits are all components of a deliberate, structured, forward-looking initiative — which is the definition of strategic planning. Strategic planning at the leadership level is the foundational support mechanism for launching a new service line. Training (A) is one tactical component of the plan, not the overarching support mechanism. Commitment to quality (C) is a value, not a strategic support function. Continuous audits (D) are an evaluation tool deployed after implementation, not during planning. Per CPHQ Quality Leadership domain standards and IHI organizational improvement frameworks, high-level strategic planning is the enabling force behind new service development and best practice adoption.

questions.text: One of the AHRQ main components?
questions.explanation: Clearinghouse for evidence based guidelines. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) serves as the primary federal clearinghouse for evidence-based clinical practice guidelines through its National Guideline Clearinghouse (NGC) and related resources. AHRQ's mission centers on producing and disseminating research evidence to improve the safety and quality of healthcare. Accreditation (A) is the function of bodies such as TJC, NCQA, and DNV GL — not AHRQ. KPI development (C) is a performance management function, not a core AHRQ component. Safety culture surveys (D) — specifically the SOPS (Surveys on Patient Safety Culture) — are an AHRQ tool, but they represent one instrument among many, not a main organizational component. The clearinghouse function is AHRQ's most defining and distinguishing role. Per AHRQ mission statements and CPHQ regulatory domain standards, evidence-based guideline dissemination is the primary AHRQ function.

questions.text: Cohesion will be which stage of team building
questions.explanation: Norming. Tuckman's model of team development identifies four sequential stages: Forming, Storming, Norming, and Performing. Cohesion — the sense of unity, mutual trust, and shared commitment among team members — develops during the Norming stage, when conflicts from the Storming phase have been resolved and the team establishes agreed-upon norms, roles, and working relationships. Forming (A) is characterized by orientation and politeness, not cohesion. Storming (B) is characterized by conflict and competition. Performing (D) is the stage of high productivity that cohesion enables, but cohesion itself emerges in Norming. Per Tuckman's team development theory and CPHQ team management domain standards, cohesion is the hallmark achievement of the Norming stage.

questions.text: Hospital develops a system (not software) to help in define problem, what from this choices we should mark the trigger as zero:

options.a: Physician not comply to hand wash hygiene

questions.explanation: Near miss error. A zero-tolerance trigger means that even a single occurrence must trigger immediate review — it is reserved for events with catastrophic harm potential where no acceptable threshold exists. A near miss error — a situation where harm was narrowly avoided — meets this criterion because it reveals a failure in a safety barrier that, had circumstances been slightly different, would have resulted in serious patient harm. Every near miss must be investigated to prevent the actual event from occurring. Hand hygiene non-compliance (A) is monitored through aggregate compliance rates, not individual zero-tolerance triggers. Incomplete medical records (B) are a documentation quality issue managed with threshold targets. Threats of suicide (D) trigger clinical risk protocols and safety interventions — but the threat itself is not categorized as a zero-tolerance quality system trigger in the same way a process near miss is. Per IHI Trigger Tool methodology, AHRQ patient safety trigger frameworks, and TJC safety standards, near miss events require zero-tolerance immediate review to prevent progression to actual harm.

questions.text: Which stage cause the team to dissolve prematurely
questions.explanation: Storming. In Tuckman's model of team development, the Storming stage is characterized by interpersonal conflict, competition for roles, resistance to the task, and power struggles. If the team is unable to navigate through the Storming stage successfully — if conflict is unresolved or leadership fails to manage the dynamics — the team may dissolve prematurely before reaching Norming and Performing. Norming (A) is when the team stabilizes — premature dissolution is unlikely here. Performing (B) is the productive stage — the team is functioning, not dissolving. Conforming (D) is not a recognized stage in Tuckman's original model. Per Tuckman's group development theory and CPHQ team management standards, Storming is the highest-risk stage for team failure and premature dissolution.

questions.text: A health organization is becoming a member in a health plan. The most important educative program to be delivered to the staff is(?).
questions.explanation: Organizational change. When a health organization joins a health plan, the primary challenge facing staff is navigating the structural, operational, and cultural changes that accompany this transition — new reporting relationships, new policies, new workflows, and integration with a larger system. Educating staff on organizational change prepares them for the disruption and gives them the tools to adapt. Conflict of interest (B) is a compliance topic applicable in certain governance or contracting situations but is not the primary educational need during integration. Consumer needs (C) and accreditation needs (D) are important but secondary — staff must first understand and adapt to the organizational changes before these other priorities can be meaningfully addressed. Per Kotter's Eight-Step Change Model, Lewin's Three-Stage Model, and CPHQ Quality Leadership standards, change management education is the most critical staff preparation during organizational transitions.

questions.text: An organization hires a quality professional to pass quality improvement concepts to the staff. The first thing the quality professional should do?

options.b: Assess the present knowledge of the staff
options.c: Review the previous performance of the staff

questions.explanation: Assess the present knowledge of the staff. Before designing or delivering any educational program, the quality professional must conduct a needs assessment — establishing the baseline knowledge level of the audience. Without this assessment, education may be pitched at the wrong level, duplicate what staff already know, or miss critical gaps. Delivering lectures immediately (A) assumes the content and level are appropriate without evidence. Reviewing previous performance (C) is a quality monitoring function, not the first step in education planning. Interviewing staff (D) may be one method of needs assessment but is not the most comprehensive first step — a formal knowledge assessment is broader and more structured. Per CPHQ educational principles, adult learning theory (Knowles' andragogy), and IHI improvement education frameworks, assessing existing knowledge is the mandatory first step before any educational intervention is designed.

questions.text: EMR prevents which type of error:
questions.explanation: Illegible handwriting. The Electronic Medical Record (EMR) — and specifically electronic physician order entry (CPOE) — most directly and definitively eliminates errors caused by illegible handwriting, which has historically been a major source of medication and care errors. When orders are entered electronically, they are always legible, timestamped, and structured. Drug interaction alerts (B) are a function of clinical decision support systems (CDSS) embedded within EMR/CPOE — a valuable but secondary feature. Administration errors (C) are primarily addressed by barcode medication administration (BCMA) systems at the point of care, not the EMR itself. Dispensing errors (D) are addressed by pharmacy automation systems. The most direct, universal, and definitional prevention that EMR provides is the elimination of handwriting illegibility errors. Per AHRQ health IT safety research and CPHQ data analytics standards, illegible handwriting elimination is the primary error-prevention function of EMR implementation.

questions.text: Which of the following tool could be used to assess the efficiency of lab specimen processing?
questions.explanation: Productivity index. Efficiency in a laboratory processing context is measured by the ratio of outputs produced to inputs consumed — which is precisely what a productivity index captures. A productivity index quantifies throughput per unit of resource (staff time, equipment use, cost) and directly measures operational efficiency of specimen processing. A Pareto chart (A) ranks causes of problems by frequency — it is useful for identifying the dominant causes of processing delays but does not measure efficiency directly. Regression analysis (B) examines statistical relationships between variables — it is an analytical tool, not an efficiency measure for operations. A profit and loss sheet (C) is a financial statement, not an operational efficiency tool. Per CPHQ health data analytics domain standards and operational management principles, a productivity index is the appropriate tool for assessing the efficiency of a defined work process like specimen processing.

questions.text: When examining the relationship between staff and patient outcomes, which of the following would be most appropriate to assess?

options.b: Patient safety data and overtime data

questions.explanation: Patient safety data and overtime data. To assess the relationship between staff factors and patient outcomes, the analysis must pair a staffing variable with a patient outcome variable. Overtime data is the most clinically relevant staffing variable — extensive research links excessive overtime to clinician fatigue, decreased vigilance, and increased adverse patient events. Patient safety data is the corresponding outcome measure. This pairing directly and validly tests the staff-to-patient outcome relationship. Option A pairs two staffing variables (overtime and absenteeism) — no patient outcome is included. Option C pairs an HR metric (turnover) with a financial metric (budget) — neither captures patient outcomes. Option D pairs two patient outcome/safety measures — no staffing variable is included. Per AHRQ nurse staffing research, NQF nurse-sensitive quality indicators, and CPHQ data analytics standards, overtime-to-patient safety data analysis is the validated approach for this relationship.

questions.text: Result of patient satisfaction survey shows some issues — what to do?

options.a: Send the report to the units with the problems
options.b: Make multidisciplinary team from the affected units

questions.explanation: Send the report to the units with the problems. When patient satisfaction survey results identify issues, the first and most targeted action is to return the data directly to the units where the problems exist. Unit-level data feedback is the essential precondition for improvement — staff and managers cannot act on problems they have not been shown. This is the first step in any data-driven improvement cycle per IHI Model for Improvement. Forming a multidisciplinary team (B) is appropriate after the units have reviewed the data and the scope of the problem is understood. Starting training (C) presupposes the cause is a knowledge or skill deficit — unproven before analysis. Sharing to the governing body (D) is appropriate for aggregate performance reporting, not the immediate action step for unit-level satisfaction issues. Per CPHQ performance improvement and quality leadership standards, returning data to the responsible unit is the first actionable step following satisfaction survey analysis.

questions.text: Who assesses the clinical competency of LIP for reappointment?
questions.explanation: Department Director. In the credentialing and privileging process, the clinical competency of a Licensed Independent Practitioner (LIP) for reappointment is assessed by the Department Director (also referred to as the Department Chief or Service Chief) — the senior clinician responsible for that practice area. This individual reviews the practitioner's OPPE data, peer review findings, case volume, clinical outcomes, and professional conduct within the department. The Governing Board (A) makes the final credentialing decision but does not perform the clinical competency assessment — it acts on recommendations. The CMO (B) oversees the medical staff broadly but does not conduct the individual competency review. The Quality Director (C) provides data and supports the process but does not assess clinical competency. Per TJC Medical Staff Standards MS.06.01.05, CPHQ credentialing domain requirements, and standard medical staff governance, the department-level clinical leader conducts the competency assessment for reappointment.

questions.text: When using cost benefit analysis in decision making it is important to remember that

options.a: A return on investment should be at least 10 to 1
options.b: Considerations of the benefits is more important than the cost
options.c: Qualitative and quantitative data should be used
options.d: Implementation costs are more important than return on investment

questions.explanation: Qualitative and quantitative data should be used. Cost-benefit analysis in healthcare must incorporate both quantitative data (measurable financial costs and outcomes) and qualitative data (patient experience, ethical considerations, staff morale, reputational impact). Relying solely on quantitative metrics misses dimensions of value that cannot be easily monetized. Option A (10:1 ROI minimum) is an arbitrary benchmark with no established basis in healthcare cost-benefit methodology. Option B is incorrect — neither cost nor benefit is categorically more important; the relationship between them is what matters. Option D inverts sound economic reasoning. Per CPHQ data analytics and decision-making standards, AHRQ economic evaluation guidance, and health economics methodology, valid cost-benefit analysis must integrate both quantitative financial data and qualitative value assessments.

questions.text: Increase aggressive behavior of patient toward the staff in (a department), what is the appropriate action:

options.a: Focus group with the staff about that

questions.explanation: Focus group with the staff about that. When a pattern of increased aggressive patient behavior is identified in a department, the quality professional's first appropriate action is to convene a focus group with the affected staff. This serves multiple purposes: it gathers frontline staff perspectives on the nature, frequency, and triggers of the aggression; it identifies gaps in current policies or processes; and it engages staff in co-designing solutions. Reviewing restraint policy (B) is a reactive, narrow response that addresses one intervention option but not the systemic problem. Informing the doctor (C) addresses individual patient management, not the departmental pattern. Escalating the treatment plan (D) is a clinical intervention for individual patients. The quality professional's role is to investigate the systemic issue through structured staff engagement before recommending policy or clinical changes. Per CPHQ quality leadership and patient safety domain standards, stakeholder engagement through structured consultation is the first step when a departmental behavioral safety pattern is identified.

questions.text: Journal identified 3 new patient safety initiatives, review the first action as quality professional:

options.a: Incorporate initiatives into organization patient safety plan
options.d: Valid data collection tool incorporate with defined data element.

questions.explanation: Incorporate initiatives into organization patient safety plan. When new patient safety initiatives are identified in the literature, the quality professional's first action is to evaluate them for organizational relevance and then incorporate applicable ones into the organization's formal patient safety plan. This ensures the initiatives are sanctioned, resourced, and aligned with organizational strategy. Collecting data (B) comes after the initiatives are planned and defined. Graphic presentation (C) is a communication/reporting step, not a first action. Developing a data collection tool (D) is a measurement planning step that follows incorporation into the safety plan. The organizational patient safety plan is the governing document that authorizes, coordinates, and resources all safety initiatives. Per TJC patient safety program requirements, IHI safety planning frameworks, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, integration into the organizational safety plan is the first formal action upon identifying new safety initiatives.

questions.text: Unwanted end-of-life services for a patient are an example of
questions.explanation: Inappropriate use of resources. Unwanted end-of-life services — procedures, interventions, or treatments provided against a patient's expressed wishes or advance directive — represent a failure to respect patient autonomy and constitute inappropriate use of resources. These services consume clinical resources (staff time, equipment, medications, ICU beds) for interventions the patient did not want and that provide no patient-centered benefit. This is not an adverse event (A) in the clinical sense — no unexpected harm from a treatment was caused; the harm is the provision of treatment itself. It is not a complication of care (B) — complications are unintended negative outcomes of care, not misalignment with patient wishes. Lack of care coordination (C) may contribute to the problem but does not define it. Per NQF's definition of overuse, IHI Triple Aim principles, and CPHQ utilization management standards, providing unwanted end-of-life interventions is the classic example of inappropriate resource use.

questions.text: Before the first team meeting, the team leader should do all of the following EXCEPT:

options.a: Draft a plan for the activities needed to complete the project and the sequence in which they should occur.
options.d: Set ground rules for team meeting

questions.explanation: Set ground rules for team meeting. Ground rules for a team are established collaboratively by the team during the first meeting — they are not set unilaterally by the team leader before the team has convened. The process of establishing ground rules is itself an early team-building activity that requires team participation to be effective and owned. All other options describe legitimate pre-meeting preparation tasks for the team leader: drafting a project activity plan (A), identifying relevant existing data (B), and arranging logistics such as location, time, and materials (C) are all appropriate pre-meeting leader responsibilities. Setting ground rules before the team meets removes the collaborative element and undermines team ownership of the process norms. Per IHI team launch methodology, Scholtes' Team Handbook, and CPHQ team management domain standards, ground rules are established in the first meeting with team participation, not preset by the leader.

questions.text: The goal of an integrated service approach is to:

options.c: Involve top management, leaders and department managers in the process
options.d: Involve all working personnel in the process

questions.explanation: Involve all working personnel in the process. An integrated service approach — rooted in total quality management and systems thinking — is defined by the engagement of all levels of the organization, from frontline workers to leadership, in the shared work of service delivery and improvement. The goal is whole-organization participation, not selective management involvement. Option C (involve top management, leaders, and department managers) describes a hierarchical, top-down approach — not integrated service. Reducing costs (A) and increasing financial return (B) may be outcomes of an effective integrated approach, but they are not the defining goal. Per Deming's 14 Points, IHI systems improvement principles, and CPHQ quality leadership standards, the integrated service approach is defined by universal staff involvement across all levels and functions.

questions.text: In general, novices, compared to experts:

options.c: Neither overrate nor underrate their diagnostic skills
options.d: Underrate or overrate their diagnostic skills according to the clinical situation

questions.explanation: Overrate their diagnostic skills. This question draws on the Dunning-Kruger effect — the well-documented cognitive bias whereby individuals with limited knowledge or skill in a domain tend to overestimate their competence. Novices lack the metacognitive awareness to accurately recognize the boundaries of their knowledge, leading to overconfidence in their diagnostic assessments. Experts, by contrast, have sufficient knowledge to recognize complexity and are often more cautious and appropriately calibrated — sometimes even underestimating their own abilities relative to peers. Option B (underrate) describes the expert pattern, not the novice pattern. Option C is empirically inaccurate. Option D introduces situational variability that is not supported by the foundational research in this area. Per cognitive psychology research (Kruger & Dunning, 1999), AHRQ diagnostic safety literature, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, novices characteristically overrate their diagnostic skills.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most likely reason for a hospital's inability to manage fluctuations in patient volume?
questions.explanation: Variation in care delivery process. Hospitals that struggle to manage fluctuations in patient volume are most often constrained by internal process variation — inconsistency in how care is delivered, how beds are managed, how discharge planning is executed, and how patient flow is coordinated. These internal process failures prevent the hospital from flexing capacity effectively in response to changing demand. Variation in demand (A) is external — hospitals cannot control when patients arrive, but they can control how they respond. Variation in physician performance (C) is a contributor but not the primary systemic reason. Patient case-mix (D) affects resource intensity but not primarily the ability to manage volume fluctuations. Per IHI patient flow improvement research, AHRQ health system capacity literature, and CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, internal process variation is the root cause of most hospital capacity management failures.

questions.text: Analysis of event trend, and customer needs is the initial phase of:
questions.explanation: Strategic planning. The initial phase of strategic planning involves an environmental scan and situational analysis — examining trends in events, stakeholder needs, market conditions, and organizational performance to inform the direction of the strategic plan. Analyzing event trends and customer needs is precisely this foundational scanning activity. Forecasting (A) is a component of strategic planning but is a more specific technical activity, not the overarching process. Resource allocation (C) occurs after strategic priorities are established, not at the beginning. Cost-benefit analysis (D) is an economic evaluation tool used to assess specific options — it is not the initial planning activity. Per CPHQ strategic planning competencies, Baldrige Excellence Framework, and organizational management standards, environmental scanning — including trend analysis and stakeholder needs assessment — is the recognized initial phase of strategic planning.

questions.text: A radiology department regularly monitors x-ray repeat/reject, timeliness of report dictation, and patient waiting times. What component is missing in this department's ongoing evaluation program?
questions.explanation: Appropriateness review. The radiology department currently monitors: repeat/reject rates (quality control of technical performance), timeliness of report dictation (process/timeliness measure), and patient waiting times (access/efficiency measure). What is conspicuously absent is an appropriateness review — an evaluation of whether the right imaging study is being ordered for the right clinical indication. Appropriateness review assesses whether diagnostic imaging is clinically indicated and aligned with evidence-based criteria, such as ACR Appropriateness Criteria. Process evaluation (B) is partially addressed through timeliness monitoring. Quality control (C) is addressed through repeat/reject rate monitoring. Documentation analysis (D) is partially addressed through dictation timeliness. The gap is the clinical appropriateness dimension — whether the right study is being done for the right reason. Per ACR practice standards, AHRQ imaging appropriateness research, and CPHQ utilization management standards, appropriateness review is the missing component in this monitoring program.

questions.text: Outside the United States, most industrialized nations offer which type of healthcare insurance?
questions.explanation: Universal coverage. The vast majority of other industrialized nations — including those in Western Europe, Canada, Australia, and Japan — provide universal healthcare coverage through government-administered or government-mandated insurance systems. This is in direct contrast to the United States, which relies on a mixed system of employer-based coverage, government programs (Medicare, Medicaid), and individual markets. Employer-based coverage (B) is a predominantly American model. Managed care (C) is a financing and delivery model used within insurance systems, not a type of national coverage. Managed competition (D) is a theoretical market model, not the dominant model in industrialized nations. Per WHO global health financing reports, CMS international health comparisons, and CPHQ health systems domain knowledge, universal coverage is the standard model for industrialized nations outside the United States.

questions.text: The most basic components of managed care include all EXCEPT

options.b: Comprehensive services at multiple levels and settings

questions.explanation: Broad choice of providers. The defining features of managed care are: prepaid financing (A) — members pay premiums in advance regardless of utilization; comprehensive services across multiple levels and settings (B) — managed care aims to coordinate care across the full continuum; and controlled access to services (C) — typically through gatekeeping by primary care physicians, prior authorization, and network restrictions. The one feature that is explicitly NOT a component of managed care is broad choice of providers (D). Managed care is fundamentally characterized by restricted provider networks — members must use in-network providers or face significantly higher costs. Broad provider choice is a feature of traditional indemnity insurance, which managed care replaced. Per NCQA managed care standards, CMS managed care program definitions, and CPHQ managed care domain standards, provider network restriction is a defining characteristic, making broad provider choice the correct "except" answer.

questions.text: In managed care, the most common form of reimbursement for primary care physicians is
questions.explanation: Capitation with withholds. Capitation is the predominant reimbursement model for primary care physicians in managed care — the PCP receives a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment for each enrolled patient regardless of the services actually rendered. The "with withholds" component means the managed care organization retains a percentage of the capitation payment (the withhold) as a risk-sharing mechanism, releasing it to the physician only if utilization targets and quality benchmarks are met. This creates a financial incentive for appropriate resource stewardship. Straight salary (A) is used in some staff-model HMOs but is not the most common managed care PCP payment model. Capitation without withholds (B) is less common because it removes the utilization incentive mechanism. Discounted fee-for-service (D) is used in PPO arrangements, not traditional managed care HMO structures. Per NCQA managed care compensation standards and CPHQ managed care domain knowledge, capitation with withholds is the most common PCP payment model in managed care.

questions.text: The probability that each step in a process will occur as it needs to occur is known as
questions.explanation: Reliability. Reliability in healthcare quality is formally defined as the probability that a system, process, or component will perform its intended function correctly under specified conditions — including the probability that each step in a process will occur as required, every time. This is the exact definition presented in the question stem. IHI defines reliability as the measurable capability of a process, procedure, or health service to perform its intended function in the required time period. Predictability (A) refers to the ability to forecast future outcomes — related but not the same as step-by-step process execution probability. Dependability (C) is a general term for trustworthiness, not a technical measurement term. Consistency (D) describes uniformity of outcomes but lacks the probabilistic precision of the reliability definition. Per IHI Reliability Framework, AHRQ patient safety research, and CPHQ performance improvement standards, reliability is the precise term for the probability of correct process step execution.

questions.text: Organizational culture most often refers to

options.a: The ethnicity of the organizations employees and licensed independent practitioner
options.b: Assumptions about people and how work gets done
options.c: The efforts to reach out to the diverse groups in the community
options.d: The scheduled social and cultural events

questions.explanation: Assumptions about people and how work gets done. Organizational culture is most accurately defined as the shared assumptions, values, beliefs, and behavioral norms that determine how members of an organization perceive, think about, and respond to their environment — including how work gets done and how people relate to each other. Edgar Schein's foundational model of organizational culture identifies underlying assumptions as the deepest and most defining layer of culture. Option A confuses organizational culture with workforce demographics or diversity characteristics. Option C describes community outreach and diversity engagement — a separate organizational function. Option D describes social events, which may reflect culture but are not its definition. Per Schein's organizational culture theory, IHI culture frameworks, and CPHQ Quality Leadership domain standards, culture is defined by the shared assumptions and behavioral norms governing how work is done.

questions.text: As quality manager to evaluate the effectiveness of dietary department you review

options.a: The timeliness of diets delivered after physician orders
options.b: The appropriateness of the nurses request to diet
options.c: The delivery of special diets ordered by physicians
options.d: Complication of the whole parental diet

questions.explanation: The timeliness of diets delivered after physician orders. Evaluating the effectiveness of a dietary department requires measuring whether the department delivers what is ordered, when it is ordered. Timeliness of diet delivery after physician orders is a direct, measurable effectiveness indicator — it captures both the accuracy of order execution and the operational performance of the dietary system. The appropriateness of nurses' requests (B) evaluates nursing practice, not dietary department effectiveness. Delivery of special diets (C) is a component of service delivery but does not specifically address timeliness, which is the key effectiveness dimension. Complications of parenteral (not "parental") diet (D) would be a patient safety/outcome measure for a specific high-risk nutrition modality — not a general departmental effectiveness measure. Per CPHQ performance improvement and measurement standards, and Donabedian's process-outcome framework, timeliness of ordered diet delivery is the appropriate process effectiveness measure for a dietary department.

questions.text: Choose the best indicators to use when determining the effectiveness of services at the emergency department (ED) in your hospital:

options.a: The number of unplanned returns to the ED
options.b: The percentage of ED patients admitted as inpatients
options.c: The patient waiting time at the ED

questions.explanation: A and B. Effectiveness of ED services is best measured by indicators that assess whether the ED achieved the right clinical outcome for the patient — not simply process efficiency. Unplanned returns to the ED (A) directly measure whether the care provided was effective — patients who return unexpectedly represent cases where the initial treatment failed to resolve the problem. The percentage of ED patients admitted as inpatients (B) reflects the acuity and clinical decision-making accuracy of the department. Together, A and B provide a balanced picture of ED clinical effectiveness. Patient waiting time (C) is an access/efficiency measure — important, but it measures throughput, not effectiveness of care delivered. Per AHRQ ED quality indicators, CMS emergency care standards, and CPHQ performance measurement domain standards, both unplanned returns and inpatient admission rates are recognized effectiveness indicators for emergency care.

questions.text: Primary role of the facilitator is to:
questions.explanation: Promote effective group dynamics. The facilitator's primary role is to promote and maintain effective group dynamics — ensuring that meetings run productively, all voices are heard, discussions stay on track, and the team's process supports its goals. The facilitator is a neutral process guide, not a content expert or decision-maker. Designing team structure (A) is a leadership or management function. Recording minutes (C) is the recorder's function — the facilitator may ensure minutes are captured but does not personally fulfill this role. Managing conflict (D, added) is a related facilitator skill but is subordinate to the overarching goal of promoting effective group dynamics. Per IHI facilitation guides, Scholtes' Team Handbook, and CPHQ team management domain standards, facilitating effective group process is the facilitator's defining primary responsibility.

questions.text: The best word explaining empowerment

options.c: Open discussion but the leader perform all important tasks

questions.explanation: Mutual trust. Empowerment in organizational and quality improvement theory is built on mutual trust — the leader trusts employees to make decisions and solve problems within their domain, and employees trust the organization to support and not penalize them for using that authority. While delegating tasks (A) is an activity that can reflect empowerment, it does not define the concept — tasks can be delegated without genuine empowerment if the employee has no real authority or psychological safety. Open discussion with the leader retaining all important decisions (C) is the opposite of empowerment — it describes a consultative but not empowering leadership style. Upward mobility (D) is a career development concept entirely unrelated to empowerment as a quality management principle. Per Deming's empowerment principles, IHI leadership frameworks, and CPHQ quality leadership domain standards, mutual trust is the foundational condition for genuine empowerment.

questions.text: The patient discharged without any counseling of his care, this problem, concerned with
questions.explanation: Transition care. A patient discharged without counseling about their care — including follow-up instructions, medication management, warning signs, and next-step appointments — represents a failure in care transitions. Transitional care encompasses all activities that support safe, effective movement of patients between care settings or from care to home, with appropriate education and handoffs. This is precisely what was missing. Medical coverage (A) relates to insurance and financing — not directly relevant here. Case management (B) coordinates care broadly but specifically addresses the transition gap through discharge counseling — the transition care framework is the broader concept that encompasses this failure. Discharge planning (D, added) is a component of transition care and is also relevant, but transition care is the overarching concept that most accurately classifies this problem. Per CMSA transition care standards, IHI care transitions framework, CMS readmission reduction initiatives, and CPHQ population health domain standards, failure to provide discharge counseling is a transition care failure.

questions.text: Your hospital adopted paperless system (EMR), when applying the program, a data was missed from the obstetrics records, your action as a CPHQ is:

options.a: Assign one member staff to enter the data
options.b: Assess the process of data entry in the system
options.c: Educate the staff about the EMR

questions.explanation: Assess the process of data entry in the system. When a newly implemented electronic system produces missing data, the quality professional's first response must be to evaluate the system and data entry process — not to assume user error or immediately default to workarounds. Missing data in a new EMR implementation is most likely caused by system design issues: required fields not enforced, workflow gaps, interface design problems, or data field mapping errors. Assigning one staff member to enter data (A) creates a bottleneck and doesn't address the root cause. Educating staff (C) presupposes the problem is user knowledge — unproven before investigation. Continuing with manual records (D) defeats the purpose of the EMR system and institutionalizes a workaround. Per AHRQ health IT safety standards, CPHQ data analytics domain principles, and standard quality improvement methodology, system process evaluation must precede any corrective action when a technology implementation produces unexpected data gaps.

questions.text: The facility makes prioritization for the problems to be solved because?

options.a: Most of hospital have not much resources to solve all together
options.b: Most of problem are meaningless to improve
options.c: Intensity of problem to be assessed

questions.explanation: Most of hospital have not much resources to solve all together. Prioritization of quality improvement problems is necessary because healthcare organizations have finite resources — staff time, financial resources, leadership attention, and improvement capacity — and cannot simultaneously address every identified problem with equal intensity. Prioritization ensures that available resources are directed toward problems with the greatest potential impact on patient safety, quality, and organizational goals. Option B is incorrect — problems are not prioritized because they are meaningless; they are prioritized because all of them have some merit but cannot all be addressed at once. Option C (intensity of problem assessment) is a criterion used in prioritization, not the reason for prioritizing. Option D (sharing with leadership) is a reporting function, not a rationale for prioritization. Per CPHQ performance improvement standards, IHI Model for Improvement, and standard QI methodology, resource limitation is the primary reason organizations must prioritize which problems to address.

questions.text: In lean method meaning of added value step

options.a: When provider change value of the process step
options.b: When provider recognize value of process
options.c: When patient recognize value of process step

questions.explanation: When patient recognize value of process step. In Lean methodology, a process step is considered value-added only when it meets three criteria: (1) the customer (patient) recognizes and cares about it; (2) it physically transforms the product or service; and (3) it is done correctly the first time. The defining criterion for value-add in Lean is the customer's (patient's) recognition of value — if the patient would not willingly pay for or benefit from the step, it is non-value-added (waste). Option A (provider changes the value) is incorrect — it is the patient, not the provider, who determines value in Lean thinking. Option B (provider recognizes value) again misidentifies who defines value. Per Lean healthcare methodology, TPS (Toyota Production System) principles, IHI Lean frameworks, and CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, value is defined from the patient's perspective — not the provider's.

questions.text: Managed competition in healthcare most often refers to:

options.a: Healthcare providers administered by competing management companies
options.b: Healthcare providers competing by type of specialty
options.c: Grouped healthcare providers competing within a geographic region

questions.explanation: Grouped healthcare providers competing within a geographic region. Managed competition is a theoretical model of healthcare market organization — developed by economist Alain Enthoven — in which groups of competing integrated healthcare delivery systems compete for enrollees within a defined geographic area, with a sponsor (such as an employer or government) structuring the competition and providing consumers with standardized information to choose among plans. The key feature is organized groups of providers competing geographically under structured rules. Option A (competing management companies) does not capture the integrated delivery system concept. Option B (competing by specialty) describes a different kind of provider competition. Option D (managed care organizations) is a broader term that encompasses many types of plans, not specifically managed competition. Per Enthoven's managed competition framework, CPHQ managed care domain standards, and health policy literature, managed competition refers to geographically organized competing provider groups.

questions.text: The interdisciplinary team is charged with creating a new admission process that will radically reduce current delays and wait times. The team is looking for
questions.explanation: Breakthrough improvement. The key phrase is "radically reduce" — this signals a goal of dramatic, step-change improvement, not incremental progress. Breakthrough improvement (also called innovation or redesign) aims for transformational gains — typically greater than 50% improvement — by fundamentally changing the process rather than incrementally optimizing it. Continuous quality improvement (A) describes an ongoing, incremental improvement philosophy — appropriate for sustaining gains, not achieving radical change. Systems thinking (B) is an analytical framework, not an improvement strategy. Process reliability (D) ensures processes work consistently — a maintenance and standardization goal, not a breakthrough goal. Per IHI Breakthrough Series methodology, CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, and Kotter's transformation framework, breakthrough improvement is the correct designation when radical, transformational change is the explicit goal.

questions.text: In the transition from quality assurance to quality management/quality improvement, which of the following emphases has resulted in the most significant benefit?

options.a: Focusing primarily on process rather than individual performance
options.b: Focusing on organization wide rather than clinical processes
options.c: Organizing activities around patient flow rather than department or discipline
options.d: Initiating more prospective rather than retrospective improvement efforts

questions.explanation: Focusing primarily on process rather than individual performance. The most significant and foundational shift in the QA-to-QI transition is the move from evaluating and blaming individual performance to analyzing and improving systems and processes. This shift — rooted in Deming's principle that 85–94% of quality problems are system-caused — is the defining characteristic of modern quality improvement and has produced the most significant benefit because it redirects improvement energy from punitive individual review to constructive system redesign. Option B is partially correct but overstates the shift — QI includes clinical processes, not just organization-wide ones. Option C (patient flow vs. departmental focus) is a real improvement in care coordination but is a secondary benefit. Option D (prospective vs. retrospective efforts) is a valid improvement but is not the most significant philosophical benefit of the QA-to-QI transition. Per Deming's 14 Points, IHI systems improvement principles, and CPHQ Quality Leadership domain standards, the process-over-individual-performance shift is the most transformative benefit.

questions.text: When incorporating lean thinking into process improvement, the quality professional teaches the team to
questions.explanation: Identify and eliminate wasteful steps. Lean thinking is fundamentally about the identification and elimination of waste (muda) — non-value-added steps in a process that consume resources without producing patient benefit. The eight categories of Lean waste (DOWNTIME: Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra-processing) are what Lean teams are trained to recognize and eliminate. Identifying suppliers and inputs (A) is part of SIPOC analysis used in Six Sigma (DMAIC), not specifically Lean. Focusing on special cause variation (B) is a statistical process control concept from Shewhart/Deming — not the primary Lean focus, which targets waste rather than variation. Considering systems structure (C) is systems thinking — a broader concept. Per IHI Lean healthcare implementation guides, Toyota Production System principles, and CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, waste identification and elimination is the defining teaching of Lean methodology.

questions.text: The following is basically reviewed to determine the medical necessity and the appropriateness of service delivery in inpatient care:
questions.explanation: Admission review. Admission review is the utilization management process specifically designed to determine whether inpatient admission is medically necessary and appropriate — evaluating whether the patient's condition requires inpatient-level care rather than outpatient or observation services. This is the primary utilization review function at the point of admission. DRG validation (B) is a coding and billing function that verifies the accuracy of diagnosis coding for payment purposes — it does not assess medical necessity of admission. Procedure review (C) evaluates the appropriateness of specific procedures, not the admission itself. Quality audits (D) are broader retrospective review activities, not specifically focused on admission necessity. Per CMS utilization review regulations, CPHQ utilization management domain standards, and InterQual/Milliman clinical review criteria, admission review is the defined mechanism for assessing inpatient admission necessity and appropriateness.

questions.text: The role of the utilization management include all EXCEPT

options.a: Care coordination and after care planning
options.c: Resource allocation: timeliness, efficiency and cost

questions.explanation: Promoting quality & patient safety. Utilization management (UM) focuses on the appropriate use of healthcare resources — reviewing medical necessity, ensuring care is provided in the right setting at the right time, coordinating care transitions, and managing resource allocation for efficiency and cost. These are all UM core functions (A, B, C). Promoting quality and patient safety (D) is the domain of the quality improvement program — it is a separate organizational function, not a core UM responsibility, even though UM and QI are linked. UM is specifically concerned with the necessity, appropriateness, and efficiency of resource use — not with the broader quality and safety agenda. Per CPHQ utilization management domain standards, URAC UM accreditation standards, and CMSA case management standards, quality and patient safety promotion falls outside the defined scope of utilization management.

questions.text: When evaluating how many people in her facility's managed care plan were able to receive the flu shot, under Dimensions of performance
questions.explanation: Availability. The question asks about how many people were able to receive the flu shot — this measures access to the service, specifically whether the vaccine was available to the population it was intended to serve. Availability as a dimension of performance assesses whether healthcare services are accessible to those who need them. Appropriateness (A) would assess whether the flu shot was the right intervention for the right patient group. Effectiveness (C) would measure whether giving the flu shot reduced flu cases. Efficacy (D) would measure the vaccine's biological ability to prevent flu under ideal conditions. The specific question — how many people received it — measures access/availability, not clinical effectiveness or biological efficacy. Per JCAHO/TJC dimensions of performance, AHRQ quality measurement frameworks, and CPHQ performance measurement standards, availability measures the degree to which healthcare is obtainable by those who need it.

questions.text: The most important patient safety issue to a utilization reviewer is

options.c: Correct assignment of diagnosis or procedure code

questions.explanation: Appropriateness of healthcare setting. From a utilization reviewer's patient safety perspective, the most critical issue is whether the patient is receiving care in the right setting — because receiving care in an inappropriate setting directly endangers patient safety. A patient who needs inpatient monitoring placed in an outpatient setting may deteriorate without appropriate surveillance; a patient held unnecessarily in an ICU may be exposed to nosocomial risks. Appropriateness of setting is the utilization reviewer's primary patient safety lens. Timeliness (A) is important but is secondary to setting appropriateness for a UR function. Medical necessity (B) is a core UM function but is framed as a coverage/payment determination — the patient safety dimension is whether the setting is right. Correct coding (C) is a billing accuracy issue, not a patient safety issue. Per CPHQ utilization management domain standards, URAC UM program requirements, and CMS conditions of participation, setting appropriateness is the utilization reviewer's most direct patient safety responsibility.

questions.text: For which aspect of care are patient-reported measures most credible?
questions.explanation: Patient-provider interactions. Patient-reported measures are most credible and valid when they assess experiences that only the patient can directly observe and report — and patient-provider interactions (communication, respect, responsiveness, information sharing) are precisely this domain. The patient is the only reliable witness to how they were treated, spoken to, and engaged by their providers. Communication between providers (A) occurs outside the patient's direct observation in many cases — the patient cannot reliably assess what providers say to each other. Adherence to clinical practice guidelines (C) requires clinical knowledge to assess — patients cannot reliably judge whether their care followed guidelines. Appropriateness of therapy (D) requires clinical judgment — not something patients can reliably evaluate without expert knowledge. Per AHRQ patient experience measurement research, HCAHPS survey design principles, and CPHQ patient safety and quality domain standards, patient-reported measures are most valid and credible for direct patient experience domains like patient-provider interaction.

questions.text: A social service department regularly monitors the number of inappropriate referrals, the timeliness of discharge planning and the number of days of discharge delays. What additional monitor should be added to evaluate the appropriateness of social service interventions?

options.a: Inadequacy of documentation in progress notes
options.c: Timeliness of referrals to social services
options.d: Number of social service referrals from nursing

questions.explanation: Attainment of social service goals. The department currently monitors three process-level indicators: referral appropriateness, discharge planning timeliness, and discharge delay frequency. What is missing is an outcome measure — specifically, whether the social service interventions actually achieved their intended goals. Attainment of social service goals (e.g., successfully placing a patient in appropriate post-acute care, connecting a patient with needed community resources) is the outcome indicator that directly evaluates whether the interventions were appropriate and effective. Inadequacy of documentation (A) is a process compliance measure, not an appropriateness/outcome indicator. Timeliness of referrals to social services (C) is another process measure — similar to what is already monitored. Number of nursing referrals (D) is a volume indicator, not an appropriateness measure. Per Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework, CMSA standards, and CPHQ performance improvement principles, outcome measurement (goal attainment) is the essential missing component in this monitoring set.

questions.text: Healthcare purchasers and payers are demanding that providers demonstrate their ability to provide high quality patient care at fair prices. Specifically, they are seeking:

options.a: Objective evidence that hospitals and other healthcare organizations manage their costs well
options.d: Objective evidence that hospitals and other healthcare organizations satisfy their customers and have desirable outcomes

questions.explanation: Objective evidence that hospitals and other healthcare organizations satisfy their customers and have desirable outcomes. The question specifically frames what purchasers and payers seek as a dual requirement: high quality AND fair prices. Option D is the only choice that simultaneously addresses both dimensions — customer satisfaction speaks to the service quality dimension, and desirable outcomes speaks to the clinical quality and value dimension. Managing costs well (A) addresses only the price side, not the quality demonstration. Current performance (B) and baseline information (C) are data types, not the specific evidence being demanded. The value-based purchasing movement — driven by CMS, large employers, and coalitions such as the Leapfrog Group — is specifically oriented toward demonstrating quality outcomes and patient satisfaction alongside cost efficiency. Per CMS value-based purchasing program standards, NCQA health plan accreditation, and CPHQ quality leadership domain standards, purchasers and payers demand objective evidence of customer satisfaction and desirable clinical outcomes.

questions.text: A healthcare facility has committed to improving the overall quality of care for patients and their families during their stay at the facility. Among these goals in improved quality of care are the goal of increased safety, better nutrition, and staff friendliness. The role of the CPHQ in improving quality of care includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.a: Providing each department of the facility with friendly reminders about patient safety
options.b: Creating a disciplinary process for staff members who fail to treat patients in a friendly way
options.c: Researching and providing the facility with different options to improve food choices
options.d: Developing an educational program to help staff members interact appropriately with patients

questions.explanation: Creating a disciplinary process for staff members who fail to treat patients in a friendly way. The CPHQ's role is to facilitate, support, and enable quality improvement — not to create or administer disciplinary systems. Disciplinary processes are a human resources and management function, not a quality professional function. The quality professional provides education (D), shares data and reminders (A), researches best practices (C), and designs improvement programs — but the punitive management of individual staff behavior is outside the CPHQ's defined scope of practice. Creating a disciplinary process is also contrary to the quality improvement philosophy of systems over individual blame. Per CPHQ scope of practice standards, IHI improvement roles, and organizational management principles, disciplinary action creation is an HR/management function explicitly outside the quality professional's role.

questions.text: The CPHQ integrates Quality findings into governance and management activities to

options.a: Align payment/incentive systems, tying rewards to clinical objectives to improve care
options.b: Maintain the current governing system to provide a continuum of care
options.c: Establish administrative policies and procedures for governance and management
options.d: Re-write the bylaws to reflect current streams of data-inclusion

questions.explanation: Align payment/incentive systems, tying rewards to clinical objectives to improve care. The CPHQ's role in integrating quality findings into governance is most powerful when it drives alignment of incentive structures with clinical quality objectives — connecting what the organization measures and values in quality to how leaders and providers are rewarded. This is the highest-leverage governance integration because it institutionalizes quality as an organizational priority through financial and recognition systems. Maintaining the current governing system (B) is status quo management — it does not describe integration of quality findings. Establishing administrative policies (C) is a management function, not specifically quality integration into governance. Re-writing bylaws (D) is a legal/governance document function that may occasionally be informed by quality but is not the purpose of quality-governance integration. Per TJC governance standards, CMS conditions of participation, and CPHQ Quality Leadership domain requirements, aligning incentives with clinical quality objectives is the defining role of quality integration at the governance level.

questions.text: The chief Executive officer of an acute care facility wishes to know the difference between Total Quality Management (TQM) and Six Sigma. The healthcare quality professional should inform him that:

options.a: TQM can be implemented on its own while the benefits of Six Sigma can only be realized when it is combined with Lean methods
options.b: TQM loosely monitors progress toward goals whereas Six sigma ensures that investment in quality produces the expected return
options.c: TQM focuses on compliance with performance standards. Six Sigma focuses on world class performance
options.d: TQM is a management philosophy whereas Six sigma is a tool to reduce variation in a process or product

questions.explanation: TQM is a management philosophy whereas Six Sigma is a tool to reduce variation in a process or product. This is the most accurate and precise distinction between TQM and Six Sigma. TQM is a comprehensive management philosophy — a cultural and organizational approach to achieving quality through continuous improvement, customer focus, and employee involvement at all levels. Six Sigma is a structured, data-driven methodology and toolkit specifically designed to reduce process variation and defects, targeting near-perfect performance (3.4 defects per million opportunities). Option A is incorrect — Six Sigma does not require Lean to deliver benefits. Option B is a distortion — TQM does not "loosely" monitor; it uses structured measurement. Option C is inaccurate — both TQM and Six Sigma aspire to excellence, but the distinction is the approach (philosophy vs. statistical methodology). Per Deming's TQM principles, Motorola's Six Sigma methodology, IHI improvement frameworks, and CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, TQM is a philosophy while Six Sigma is a variation-reduction methodology and toolkit.

questions.text: Total Quality Management (TQM) can affect all of the following significant changes in organizational functions EXCEPT:

options.a: Diminishing of the top management role
options.d: An emphasis on individuals involvement in process management and continuous improvement

questions.explanation: Diminishing of the top management role. TQM does not diminish the role of top management — it transforms and intensifies it. Deming's 14 Points explicitly place the primary responsibility for quality on leadership — senior leaders must model quality values, remove barriers, and commit resources. TQM requires active, visible, and sustained top management engagement. Customer satisfaction (B) is a central TQM principle. Reducing hierarchical structure (C) occurs in TQM as teams are empowered and traditional command-and-control structures give way to flatter, more collaborative models. Individual involvement in process management and continuous improvement (D) is another core TQM principle. The one thing TQM does not do is diminish top management's role — it transforms that role from directive authority to quality champion and system steward. Per Deming's 14 Points, Juran's quality trilogy, and CPHQ Quality Leadership domain standards, top management commitment is amplified, not diminished, under TQM.

questions.text: To achieve excellence of care under TQM philosophy, healthcare organizations must ensure:

options.a: Cautious use of minimal standards of care

questions.explanation: None of the above. TQM philosophy explicitly rejects the goal of merely meeting or working within minimal standards. The essence of TQM is the pursuit of continuous improvement and excellence — going beyond minimum compliance to constantly raise the bar. Cautious use of minimal standards (A) is a compliance mindset, not a TQM mindset. Meeting minimal standards (B) is the floor, not the ceiling — TQM demands aspiration beyond floors. Ignoring minimal standards (C) is reckless and not what TQM advocates. TQM requires organizations to exceed standards, drive toward zero defects, and continuously improve — making all three options individually wrong and "None of the above" the correct answer. Per Deming's 14 Points, Juran's quality planning principles, IHI improvement philosophy, and CPHQ quality leadership standards, excellence under TQM requires transcending minimal standards through continuous improvement.

questions.text: In one of the first class high quality hospitals in Newcastle, Ministry of Health yield a survey about what is the impact of safe culture of work on the caregivers? As a quality man, what is not expected to find in the final report of the survey?

options.a: The staff did not worry that their mistakes will be reported in their personnel file.
options.b: The staff belief that their weakness points will not be used against them
options.c: The highest percentage of staff reported that no significant adverse events had occurred in their setting during the past 12 months
options.d: Low average composite score involved questions related to non-punitive response to error

questions.explanation: The highest percentage of staff reported that no significant adverse events had occurred in their setting during the past 12 months. This question asks what would NOT be expected in a strong safety culture survey report. Options A, B, and D all represent positive safety culture indicators: staff not fearing personnel repercussions (A), staff trusting that weaknesses won't be weaponized against them (B), and low non-punitive response scores being flagged as a concern (D) — all are expected findings in safety culture analysis. Option C, however, is a red flag, not a positive indicator. In a genuine high-safety-culture environment, staff actively report near misses and adverse events — high reporting rates are a sign of trust and transparency. A claim that very few adverse events occurred is more consistent with under-reporting (a safety culture failure) than with actual safety. Per AHRQ Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture (HSOPS), IHI safety culture frameworks, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, high adverse event reporting rates are expected in strong safety cultures — not low ones.

questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to be a benefit of concurrent ambulatory surgical case review

options.a: Decreased medical record review at discharge
options.b: An increase in the number of cases failing screening criteria

questions.explanation: Decreased medical record review at discharge. Concurrent review — conducted during the episode of care rather than after discharge — allows issues to be identified and resolved in real time. A primary benefit of concurrent ambulatory surgical case review is that problems identified and corrected during the procedure or visit reduce the need for extensive retrospective medical record review at discharge, because documentation and compliance issues have already been addressed. An increase in cases failing screening criteria (B) is an intermediate finding, not a benefit — it means more problems are being caught, but it is a finding, not the benefit. Increased reviewer competence (C) may occur over time but is not a direct or primary benefit of concurrent review. Decreased employee turnover (D) is an HR outcome with no logical direct connection to concurrent case review methodology. Per CPHQ utilization management and performance improvement domain standards, concurrent review's primary operational benefit is reduction in retrospective workload by addressing issues during care delivery.

questions.text: Deploying a CQI team would be first approach in addressing which

options.a: Several patient complained their call lights not answered during night shifts
options.b: Several physicians don't allocate enough time for procedures which booking surgical cases
options.c: Finance billing outpatient procedures as ambulatory surgery
options.d: Results of preadmission testing for inpatient survey are unavailable 35% of time causing delays

questions.explanation: Results of preadmission testing for inpatient survey are unavailable 35% of time causing delays. A CQI team approach is most appropriate when the problem is a systems and process issue — one that is recurring, measurable, involves multiple departments or steps, and requires cross-functional analysis and redesign. Preadmission testing results being unavailable 35% of the time causing delays is precisely this type of problem: it is measurable, it recurs consistently, it involves multiple departments (lab, radiology, admissions, scheduling), and it requires process redesign — the ideal CQI team mandate. Call lights not being answered (A) is a staffing and accountability issue that a nurse manager or unit director should address directly. Physician scheduling behavior (B) is a medical staff behavior issue requiring physician engagement through peer leadership, not a CQI team. Finance billing coding (C) is a compliance and billing accuracy issue, not a CQI improvement problem. Per IHI Model for Improvement, CPHQ performance improvement standards, and CQI team deployment criteria, multi-departmental, measurable, process-level problems are the appropriate target for CQI team deployment.

questions.text: An ambulatory outpatient care facility identifies an opportunity to improve the turnaround time for reports of x-rays performed at a local hospital. Which of the following groups should be involved in the team to improve the process?

options.b: Primary care physician, clinic nurse, and clinic administrator
options.c: Radiologist, primary care physician, and clinic medical records
options.d: Clerical, clinical and administrative staff from both facilities

questions.explanation: Clerical, clinical and administrative staff from both facilities. X-ray report turnaround time is a cross-institutional, cross-functional process involving multiple steps and multiple types of staff at both the outpatient clinic and the hospital. The process spans clinical (radiology read, physician review), administrative (order entry, report routing, scheduling), and clerical (filing, communication, document management) functions at both facilities. A team that only includes staff from one facility (B, C) or only administrative representatives (A) would miss critical process steps and perspectives. The only team composition that covers the full scope of the problem — all disciplines and both facilities — is D. Per IHI team selection principles, CPHQ performance improvement domain standards, and cross-organizational process improvement methodology, the team must represent every step and every stakeholder in the process being improved.

questions.text: Pre-authorization is required for all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Ambulatory care. Pre-authorization (prior authorization) is a utilization management requirement for services that involve significant resource use, cost, or clinical risk — typically inpatient admissions (A), rehabilitation admissions (C), and psychiatric inpatient care (D). Routine ambulatory care visits (B) — such as standard outpatient physician visits and routine diagnostic tests — typically do not require pre-authorization in most managed care plans. While some specialized ambulatory procedures may require authorization, general ambulatory care is exempt from pre-authorization requirements as a standard policy. Per URAC utilization management standards, CMS managed care authorization requirements, and CPHQ utilization management domain standards, routine ambulatory care is generally excluded from pre-authorization requirements.

questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding the JCAHO's no smoking policy?

options.a: Exceptions to the prohibitions are usually determined by licensed, independent practitioners
options.b: Social rehabilitation settings may not require a licensed independent practitioner's order
options.c: Exceptions are allowed in hospital sponsored ambulatory care areas
options.d: Exceptions are not allowed in adolescent and child patient care areas

questions.explanation: Exceptions are allowed in hospital sponsored ambulatory care areas. TJC (formerly JCAHO) has a comprehensive no smoking policy that applies to all areas of accredited organizations, including hospital-sponsored ambulatory care areas. Exceptions are not broadly allowed in ambulatory care settings — the policy is facility-wide. Option A is true: where exceptions exist (e.g., for specific patient populations with clinical justification), they require a licensed independent practitioner's order. Option B is true: social rehabilitation settings have specific provisions that may differ. Option D is true: exceptions are explicitly not allowed in pediatric and adolescent patient care areas — these are protected zones with zero exceptions. The statement in Option C — that exceptions are allowed in hospital-sponsored ambulatory care — is incorrect as a general rule. Per TJC EC (Environment of Care) standards and the TJC tobacco-free environment policy, the no smoking policy applies to all settings including ambulatory care, making C the false statement.

questions.text: It is difficult to predict outcomes of care in
questions.explanation: Emergency care. Emergency care presents the greatest challenge for predicting outcomes because patients arrive with unknown histories, acute and often rapidly changing conditions, incomplete information, and without the pre-visit assessment and planning available in other settings. The unpredictability of the chief complaint, severity, and trajectory is maximum in the emergency setting. Ambulatory care (A) involves scheduled, planned, lower-acuity encounters where patient history is known — outcomes are more predictable. Hospital care (B) involves a structured admission process with workup and monitoring — outcomes can be tracked and managed. Intensive care (C) involves critically ill patients but within a highly monitored, protocol-driven environment that enables outcome prediction and management. Per AHRQ emergency care quality research, CPHQ patient safety domain standards, and clinical care setting characteristics, the ED's inherent unpredictability makes it the most challenging setting for outcome prediction.

questions.text: Which of the following group is least likely to report errors?
questions.explanation: Independent contractor. Independent contractors — physicians or other clinicians who are not employed by the organization and do not have the same organizational relationship, accountability structures, or psychological investment in the institution — are least likely to report errors. They may not feel bound by the organization's reporting culture, may fear liability exposure without the protection of an employment relationship, and may have less familiarity with reporting systems. Primary care physicians (A) and nurses (D), while also sometimes hesitant to report, are more integrated into the organizational structure and face more direct accountability. Support staff (B) are generally embedded in the organizational culture and reporting systems. Per AHRQ error reporting research, IHI safety culture literature, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, workforce members who are least integrated into the organizational culture — such as independent contractors — have the lowest error reporting rates.

questions.text: Hospital infection control policies generally require

options.a: 100% Concurrent surveillance for healthcare associated infection tracking
options.b: Periodic monitoring of staff and equipment for AIDs
options.c: Coordination of activities in patient care, ancillary, and support services
options.d: That the infection control committee be a medical staff committee

questions.explanation: Coordination of activities in patient care, ancillary, and support services. Hospital infection control programs are organizationally defined by their cross-departmental coordinating function — bringing together patient care, ancillary services (laboratory, radiology, pharmacy), and support services (environmental services, dietary, laundry) under a unified infection prevention strategy. This coordination function is a standard requirement of TJC infection control standards and CDC infection prevention guidelines. 100% concurrent surveillance (A) is impractical and not required — surveillance is typically targeted and risk-based, not 100% concurrent. Periodic monitoring for AIDS specifically (B) is not an infection control policy requirement — the reference to AIDS is outdated and overly specific. Requiring the infection control committee to be a medical staff committee (D) is not a universal requirement — infection control committees are typically multidisciplinary and report to quality or administration, not exclusively to the medical staff. Per TJC IC (Infection Control) standards, CDC HICPAC guidelines, and CPHQ patient safety domain standards, cross-departmental coordination is the defining organizational requirement of infection control programs.

questions.text: Confidentiality of information is best accomplished by

options.c: Having all staff sign a confidentiality agreement
options.d: Remove all patient and practitioner identifiers from documents

questions.explanation: Limiting access. The most effective and foundational mechanism for protecting the confidentiality of information is limiting access — ensuring that only individuals who have a legitimate need to know can access protected information. This is the primary principle underlying HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules, which require role-based access controls for electronic protected health information (ePHI). Obtaining consent to release (B) is required when sharing information externally but does not protect it within the organization from unauthorized internal access. Staff confidentiality agreements (C) are administrative safeguards that create legal accountability but do not physically restrict access. De-identification (D) removes identifiers but transforms data in a way that may not be applicable to active patient records. Per HIPAA Privacy Rule requirements, AHRQ health information privacy standards, and CPHQ data management domain standards, access limitation (role-based access control) is the primary and most effective confidentiality protection mechanism.

questions.text: The part of documentation for medical staff peer review that is most often missing is:
questions.explanation: Follow-up/evaluation of action effectiveness. Medical staff peer review documentation commonly captures findings and conclusions (A), makes recommendations (B), and documents the action taken (C) — these three elements are relatively consistently present. What is most frequently and critically absent is the follow-up step: evaluating whether the action taken actually produced the intended improvement. Without this closing loop, peer review becomes a documentation exercise rather than a quality improvement mechanism. The follow-up and effectiveness evaluation is the outcome measurement that determines whether the peer review process is producing real change in clinical performance. Per TJC Medical Staff Standards, CPHQ credentialing and peer review domain standards, and standard peer review program design, failure to close the loop with action effectiveness evaluation is the most common and consequential documentation gap in peer review programs.

questions.text: Which of the following are essential functions of an infection control program
